questions.prompt: In Configuration Management, which statement best describes Centralized configuration?
options: Return the same success response for every request regardless of outcome.
Keep configuration centralized and validate required settings at startup. Store request-specific values in request-scoped state and never place user-specific secrets in shared application locals.
Validate required configuration at startup, keep credentials outside source control, expose a limited health check, and verify logs, deployment smoke tests and recovery steps before release.
Move all backend decisions into the browser and trust the submitted values.
questions.answer_key: Keep configuration centralized and validate required settings at startup. Store request-specific values in request-scoped state and never place user-specific secrets in shared application locals.
questions.explanation: Keep configuration centralized and validate required settings at startup. Store request-specific values in request-scoped state and never place user-specific secrets in shared application locals.

questions.prompt: Which design rule is most appropriate when applying Configuration Management?
options: Separate HTTP handling from business rules, persistence, and integration clients. Dependency injection and consistent contracts make modules easier to test; avoid abstractions that hide control flow.
Trust request fields and skip authorization to keep handlers small.
Suppress all errors without recording safe diagnostic information.
Assume that adding CORS makes private routes authenticated.
questions.answer_key: Separate HTTP handling from business rules, persistence, and integration clients. Dependency injection and consistent contracts make modules easier to test; avoid abstractions that hide control flow.
questions.explanation: Separate HTTP handling from business rules, persistence, and integration clients. Dependency injection and consistent contracts make modules easier to test; avoid abstractions that hide control flow.

questions.prompt: A change related to Configuration Management appears to work for one normal request. What is the strongest next verification step?
options: Test only one successful request manually and record no expected output.
Use production data to avoid building a small reproducible fixture.
Treat the page’s displayed reference output as proof that Node.js executed the code.
Use repeatable tests for a successful request and at least one invalid/boundary or dependency-failure case.
questions.answer_key: Use repeatable tests for a successful request and at least one invalid/boundary or dependency-failure case.
questions.explanation: Use repeatable tests for a successful request and at least one invalid/boundary or dependency-failure case.
